juce::ValueTree Class Referencefinal

## Detailed Description

A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo and redo behaviour.

A [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") contains a list of named properties as var objects, and also holds any number of sub-trees.

Create [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") objects on the stack, and don't be afraid to copy them around, as they're simply a lightweight reference to a shared data container. Creating a copy of another [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") simply creates a new reference to the same underlying object - to make a separate, deep copy of a tree you should explicitly call [createCopy()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html#abd436eb86badef40713c6a28e8ccce84 "Returns a deep copy of this tree and all its sub-trees.").

Each [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") has a type name, in much the same way as an [XmlElement](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1XmlElement.html "Used to build a tree of elements representing an XML document.") has a tag name, and much of the structure of a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") is similar to an [XmlElement](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1XmlElement.html "Used to build a tree of elements representing an XML document.") tree. You can convert a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") to and from an [XmlElement](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1XmlElement.html "Used to build a tree of elements representing an XML document."), and as long as the XML doesn't contain text elements, the conversion works well and makes a good serialisation format. They can also be serialised to a binary format, which is very fast and compact.

All the methods that change data take an optional [UndoManager](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1UndoManager.html "Manages a list of undo/redo commands."), which will be used to track any changes to the object. For this to work, you have to be careful to consistently always use the same [UndoManager](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1UndoManager.html "Manages a list of undo/redo commands.") for all operations to any sub-tree inside the tree.

A [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") can only be a child of one parent at a time, so if you're moving one from one tree to another, be careful to always remove it first, before adding it. This could also mess up your undo/redo chain, so be wary! In a debug build you should hit assertions if you try to do anything dangerous, but there are still plenty of ways it could go wrong.

Note that although the children in a tree have a fixed order, the properties are not guaranteed to be stored in any particular order, so don't expect that a property's index will correspond to the order in which the property was added, or that it will remain constant when other properties are added or removed.

Listeners can be added to a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") to be told when properties change and when sub-trees are added or removed.

See also[var](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1var.html "A variant class, that can be used to hold a range of primitive values."), [XmlElement](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1XmlElement.html "Used to build a tree of elements representing an XML document.")

juce::ValueTree Class Referencefinal

Detailed Description

A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo and redo behaviour.

A ValueTree contains a list of named properties as var objects, and also holds any number of sub-trees.

Create ValueTree objects on the stack, and don't be afraid to copy them around, as they're simply a lightweight reference to a shared data container. Creating a copy of another ValueTree simply creates a new reference to the same underlying object - to make a separate, deep copy of a tree you should explicitly call createCopy().

Each ValueTree has a type name, in much the same way as an XmlElement has a tag name, and much of the structure of a ValueTree is similar to an XmlElement tree. You can convert a ValueTree to and from an XmlElement, and as long as the XML doesn't contain text elements, the conversion works well and makes a good serialisation format. They can also be serialised to a binary format, which is very fast and compact.

All the methods that change data take an optional UndoManager, which will be used to track any changes to the object. For this to work, you have to be careful to consistently always use the same UndoManager for all operations to any sub-tree inside the tree.

A ValueTree can only be a child of one parent at a time, so if you're moving one from one tree to another, be careful to always remove it first, before adding it. This could also mess up your undo/redo chain, so be wary! In a debug build you should hit assertions if you try to do anything dangerous, but there are still plenty of ways it could go wrong.

Note that although the children in a tree have a fixed order, the properties are not guaranteed to be stored in any particular order, so don't expect that a property's index will correspond to the order in which the property was added, or that it will remain constant when other properties are added or removed.

Listeners can be added to a ValueTree to be told when properties change and when sub-trees are added or removed.
